## I.C.E. in LA

Since June 6th, 2025, the citizens of Los Angeles as well as other major American cities, have taken to the streets in an attempt to push ICE out of their cities. These ongoing events in California have caused the National Guard to be deployed in the Golden State without the approval of Governor Gavin Newsom. The question is, what is ICE? And what do you do if they come knocking?

## What is I.C.E and why are people protesting?

ICE stands for Immigration and Customs Enforcement. ICE enforces federal laws by controlling borders, customs, trade, and immigration. The organization was formed in 2003 under the Bush administration via a merger of the Investigative and the Interior Enforcement departments of the National Customs, Immigration, and Naturalization Service. ICE has 3 branches: HSI (Homeland Security Investigations), ERO (Enforcement and Removal Operations), and OPLA (Office of the Principal Legal Advisor). The ERO, which is the main branch in this case is the branch that carries out the deportation of undocumented citizens. The OPLA is the largest legal office in the Dep of Homeland Security and serves as the exclusive representative of the department in deportation proceedings before the Executive Office of Immigration Review. The HSI is the main investigative unit of the Dep of Homeland Security via investigating and dismantling transnational criminal organizations that threaten the safety of the United States.

## Why are people protesting?

Since Trump took office in early 2025, the number of citizens protesting deportations has gone up, and these are the possible explanations for this public outcry.

Many immigrants are being sent to ‘third countries’ rather than their country of origin.

Undocumented immigrants are being deported and charged without due process, which directly goes against the Constitution.

Due process is the right to a fair trial. Anyone tried in a court of law in the United States, regardless of their citizenship, is guaranteed to a fair and speedy trial in which they are allowed to either submit or contest their charges in a proper court of law.

Citizens and immigrants with documentation are being deported.

Immigrants are being baited into their arrests via ICE officers luring them under the guise of immigration proceedings and hearings.

## If you are undocumented and you encounter ICE

IMPORTANT: STAY CALM.

You are allowed to ask ICE officers for their name and badge number.

Prepare yourself and your family for the worst-case scenario, and if possible, find an immigration attorney and memorize (or write down) their number along with other emergency contacts. Since this is not a criminal situation, the government does not have to provide you with an attorney.

TELL THE TRUTH. While it is within your rights to stay silent if you are detained, if you choose to speak, you must tell the truth.

DO NOT DO ANYTHING WITHOUT CONSULTING YOUR LAWYER: They are the professionals in this situation and are able to look at the situation you are in through a clear lens.

## If they show up at your place of work/residency

If they dont have a warrant signed by a judge, DO NOT LET THEM IN.

If they knock on your door, wait for them to produce the warrant before you fully open your door.

## If you are outside

Move to a safe space and make sure you are not being followed.

If you are a U.S. citizen, it is within your rights to ask for an officer’s name and ID number and record them during an arrest. This is protected under your First Amendment rights.

If you are at an airport and encounter customs officers, they can only question you about your identity and your status as a citizen. If you refuse to answer these questions, you might have your entry delayed but officers cannot deny your entry unless if you are non-citizen visa holder.

IMPORTANT: ALWAYS ASK IF YOU ARE BEING DETAINED. ‘OFFICER, AM I BEING DETAINED?’ BE SURE TO POLITELY ASK THEM.

## Judicial vs. administrative warrants

Sample of judicial warrant: ICE can enter your home. Check that the warrant has your correct name and address. A search warrant is needed to search and enter premises; and administrative warrant doesn’t allow entry. Officers typically can only search the specified person or property described. The search is only allowed at the stated time and date. A warrant is only valid with a judge’s signature. Without it, you can refuse the search.

Sample of administrative warrant: ICE cannot enter your home. Important: An administrative warrant allows for the arrest of the person named, NOT a search of private property. You can refuse if an officer tries to search your home with this warrant. This warrant is valid only for the arrest of the person named. It must be signed by an immigration officer to be valid.

## How can you spread awareness? Ways to get involved

Volunteer or apply for internships with immigrant advocacy organizations.

Support he ICE Out of Courts Campaign — aim to prevent ICE presence in courthouses.

Share and distribute materials both online and in public spaces (Schools, libraries, community centers).

Help community members create emergency plans (contacts, child custody, legal aid).

Engage in local and state advocacy to protect immigrant communities.

## How to defend your community

Help community members create emergency plans (contacts, child custody, legal aid).

Clarify what kind of immigration case they may face and possible legal strategies.

Stay informed about Operation Palladium and other ICE programs via FOIA-released documents.

## Acknowledge the law and use your rights! Free speech and protest rights

You may: Protest, chant, picket, distribute flyers in public areas (sidewalks, plazas, parks).

Protected under the First Amendment as long as you: Do not block entrances/sidewalks. Do not disrupt counter protests. Do not incite to violence or spread obscene/knowingly false speech.

Marching in the streets: Usually requires a permit. Must follow traffic laws.

Public areas allows protected speech while, private property has limited or no free speech unless allowed.

## Law enforcement encounters

Everyone, regardless of immigration status, has these rights: Right to remain silent. Right to refuse consent to searches. Right to an attorney if arrested.

If stopped by the police: Stay calm. Don’t run. Ask: ‘Am I free to leave?’ If yes, you may walk away.

In a vehicle stop: Drivers must show license, registration, and insurance. Passengers may remain silent and ask if they can leave. Police may only search the vehicle if they suspect it contains evidence of a crime.

## Take action and use these resources! Know your rights ‘Red Cards’

Distributed by LAUSD for immigrant families. Created by immigrant Legal Resource Center. Wallet-sized cards explaining rights. Available to both citizens and non-citizen. Offered in 16 languages (e.g., Spanish, Haitian, Creole, Tigrinya).
